sections.content:
Key topics of calculus include: differentiation and integration of trigonometric, exponential and
logarithmic functions, graphing, optimization, and probability.
Key topics of statistics and probability include: basic theory and applications of various discrete
and continuous probability distributions, random sampling techniques including confidence
intervals and hypothesis testing.

sections.content:
MATH 1005 Calculus and Statistics is a 4-credit applied course that combines a lighter treatment of single-variable calculus with introductory probability and statistics. It is designed for students who have only HKDSE Compulsory Mathematics (Level 2+) and have not taken (or scored high on) M1/M2. For BMH students it is one of the allowed options alongside MATH 1006 and MATH 1013.
What
sections.teaching: MATH 1005 teaching is quite boring. Lectures are large-class, example-driven walkthroughs of standard techniques with little discussion, few surprising applications, and almost no attempt to make the statistics half feel connected to real biomedical data. The pace is steady rather than engaging, tutorials mainly drill extra problems, and the overall style rewards sitting quietly and copying methods rather than thinking out loud. It gets the syllabus covered, but it rarely holds attention.
sections.grading: MATH 1005 grading is not particularly harsh. The course uses criterion-referenced marking rather than a curve, homework is a reliable 15%, and you can drop a weak midterm so that the final counts 85% instead. Combined with relatively straightforward WeBWorK and published grade descriptors that treat solid computational competence as enough for a B or better, most students who keep up with practice can pass comfortably and have a realistic shot at a decent letter grade without needing exceptional insight.
sections.workload: MATH 1005 workload is easy and light on homework. WeBWorK is the main regular assignment and usually takes only a short session each time if you stay current; there are no heavy written problem sets or projects. Lectures plus one tutorial a week plus exam revision are enough for most students, so the course does not pile on extra work beyond what is needed to practise the techniques.

sections.content:
The course covers differentiation, integration, probability, and statistics. It can be seen as a simplified combination of LANG 1013 and ISOM 2500. The scope is relatively broad, but none of the topics go very deep. Overall, it works more as a general quantitative foundation course rather than one that focuses on rigorous theory.

The calculus part of the course focuses mainly on conceptual understanding and basic applications. For differentiation and integration, the methods used are limited to the chain rule, the substitution rule, and integration by parts. The emphasis is on knowing when and how to apply these tools.

The probability section is more structured and covers standard topics such as probability, conditional probability, discrete random variables, and continuous random variables. Compared to calculus, this part goes slightly deeper and forms a more complete framework.

The statistics component focuses on inferential statistics, including parameter estimation and hypothesis testing.
sections.teaching: Professor Yaojing teaches in a very detailed and clear manner. The lectures are well-paced and easy to follow, and he is quite responsible as an instructor. Explanations are thorough, and the logic behind formulas and methods is usually made explicit. Overall, the teaching quality is solid and reliable.
sections.grading:
There are two assessment schemes, both of which use absolute grading.

Scheme 1
Homework: 15%
Midterm Exam: 25%
Final Exam: 60%

Scheme 2
Homework: 15%
Midterm Exam: 0%
Final Exam: 85%

The flexibility between the two schemes is helpful. For reference, I scored 50/50 on the midterm and 93/100 on the final, which resulted in a final letter grade of A+.
sections.workload: The workload is very light. Homework is straightforward, with unlimited attempts and no penalty for re-submission. The midterm is also very easy, consisting of 16 multiple-choice questions, and around half of the students had already left the exam room within the first 20 minutes. The final exam is noticeably more difficult than the midterm and requires some revision. Most of the workload comes from the second half of the course, where the concepts take slightly more time to fully understand.
